observations.title: Accounting errors in recording cash-in-bank (CiB) transactions amounting to P66.815 million resulted in the misstatement of affected CiB accounts and weighed on the fair presentation of these accounts in the City’s Fg Statements (FS).
observations.description:
1.1 The International Public Sector Accounting Standards (IPSAS) requires that FS shall present fairly the financial position, financial performance and cash flows of an entity. Fair presentation requires the faithful presentation of the effects of transactions, other events and conditions in accordance with the definitions and recognition criteria for assets, liabilities, income and expenses set out in the IPSAS.

1.2 Each government agency shall record its financial transactions and operations conformably with the generally accepted accounting principles and in accordance with pertinent laws, rules and regulations.

1.3 On a test basis and based on the financial records submitted by the City, we performed such standard audit procedures as review, examination, verification and analysis (among others) of the accounts presented in the City’s FS. The audit showed the accounting errors in Table 1 totaling P66,815,141.99 which resulted in the misstatement of account balances/carrying amounts.

| Table 1 - Accounting errors |  |
| --- | --- |
| Error Description | Amount |
| Checks issued not captured in the books of accounts | P5,912,799.87 |
| Net overstatement on account of unrecognized deposits, withdrawals and other errors – General Fund (GF) | 51,206,855.06 |
| Net understatement on account of unrecognized withdrawals, credit memos and debit memos and other errors – Trust Fund (TF) | 9,695,487.06 |
| Total accounting errors | P66,815,141.99 |
| Percentage of total assets of P74,463,048,644.70 | 0.09 |

Checks issued not recognized in the books – P5.913 million

1.4 The City maintained 83 bank accounts in CY 2020, as shown in Table 2.

| Table 2 - Number of bank accounts maintained by the City of Manila in CY 2020 |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Account | GF | Special Education Fund (SEF) | TF | Total |
| Cash in Bank-Local Currency Current Account (CiB-LCCA) | 5 | 1 | 10 | 16 |
| CiB-LCCA Expropriation Accounts | 52 | - | - | 52 |
| CiB-Local Currency Time Deposit (CiB-LCTD) | 6 | 3 | 5 | 14 |
| CiB-Foreign Currency Savings Account (CiB-FCSA) | - | - | 1 | 1 |
| Total | 63 | 4 | 16 | 83 |

1.5 Section 43 of Manual on the New Government Accounting System for Local Government Units (MNGAS for LGUs) provides:

“Reporting of Checks Issued. – The checks released to claimants shall be reported in the Report of Checks Issued (RCI) which shall be prepared daily by the Treasurer for each fund. It shall be submitted to the Accountant for preparation of Journal of Entry Voucher based on individual checks issued and recording in the Check Disbursements Journal (CkDJ).”

1.6 Our audit showed that 6,169 checks issued for a total of P5,912,799.87 were recorded in the RCI but not recognized in the CkDJ contrary to Section 43 of MNGAS for LGUs.

1.7 This came about mainly because of the: (a) absence of an effective reconciliation of the records of the Office of the City Accountant (OCAT) and City Treasurer’s Office; (b) inability of the accounting application used by the OCAT (PPSAS System) to capture the standard transaction description and references and produce the prescribed primary and subsidiary records that provide the audit trail; and (c) breakdown of the bank reconciliation as reconciling items are either not acted upon timely or not acted upon at all. These causes are evident in the accounting/control deficiencies discussed in the succeeding sub-paragraphs.

a. Checks issued were not captured in CkDJ because checks issued by batch were not sequentially recorded in the CkDJ and only the first check number of the batch was captured therein.

b. There were checks recorded in the CkDJ but not found in the appertaining RCI (Table 3). Available information/documents did not permit the Audit Team to establish, among others, if these are mere errors in encoding or if these were in fact checks issued not captured in the RCI.

Table 3 - Checks recorded in the CkDJ but not found in the appertaining RCI

| Fund | Quantity | Amount |
| --- | --- | --- |
| SEF | 16 | P38,044,991.07 |
| TF | 10 | 1,026,059.37 |
| Total | 26 | P39,071,050.44 |

1.8 The causes of the accounting errors enumerated in para. 1.7 have been communicated to the City through the 2019 Annual Audit Report (Finding Nos. 2 and 4). These causes have been reiterated/discussed with the responsible officials during the course of the audit of the City’s 2020 accounts.

Net overstatement/understatement on account of unrecognized deposits, withdrawals, credit memos and debit memos and other errors - P60.902 million

1.10 We looked into the book reconciling items of P51,206,855.06 and P9,695,487.06 under the GF and TF, respectively, listed in the City’s Banks Reconciliation Statements (BRS). These book reconciling items pertain to transactions in CYs 2014 to 2020 and are errors in accounting for the CiB the OCAT itself identified.

1.11 Review and verification of the BRS revealed that, contrary to procedures prescribed under COA Circular No. 96-011, journal vouchers to record all valid reconciling items requiring adjustments and corrections are not promptly prepared by the OCAT.

1.12 We emphasized that the preparation of BRS is not just finding the amounts of discrepancies in order to reconcile both records but to investigate the propriety of each reconciling items and to effect promptly the necessary adjustments in the books.

recommendations.label: a.
recommendations.text: Prepare the adjusting entry to record the 6,169 checks with a total amount of P5.913 million in the CkDJ; and

recommendations.label: b.
recommendations.text: Adopt preventive and corrective measures to address the deficiencies noted in Paragraph no. 1.7.
We recommended that Management submit supporting documents as basis for recording of the transactions from CYs 2014 to CY 2020 in the amount of P60.902 million.

observations.title: Deficiencies in accounting for PPE undermine the quality of PPE information presented in the City’s FS.
observations.description:

2.2 The foregoing accounting deficiencies came about mainly because of the breakdown in the operation of the PPE reconciliation. While physical inventory was conducted for most of the PPE, the results were not fully reconciled with the recognized accountabilities, thus, accounting deficiencies, among others, were not timely detected and corrected. It must be emphasized that the operation of control in PPE reconciliation is neither in the conduct of the physical inventory nor in the comparison of records but in addressing the issues found during such reconciliation.

2.3 The breakdown in the operation of the PPE reconciliation is also evident in the following:

2.3.1 There are items of PPE recognized in the accounting and property records in bulk amount and counted as a single unit of PPE, thus, tracking them and establishing accountability using these records is extremely difficult if not practically impossible (Table 7);

| Total SEF | 8 | P636,542,199.80 |
| Grand Total | 22 | P740,330,745.99 |

2.3.2 The following information are NOT in the PPE records (Table 8) which rendered tracking and establishing accountability for the PPE arduous and inefficient;

Table 8 - PPE information Not in the PPE Records

| --- | --- |

2.3.3 The condition of most of the PPE is not specified in the inventory records which raises valuation and PPE management issues.

recommendations.label: a.
recommendations.text: Provide depreciation for the 4,087 depreciable PPE items totaling P10.263 billion;

recommendations.label: b.
recommendations.text: In the absence of documents establishing the acquisition cost of four PPE items with nominal costs totaling P20,061.43, measure these PPE using their fair value and disclose the valuation in the Notes to FS;

recommendations.label: c.
recommendations.text: Record PPE individually in the PPE records (para. 2.3.1); and

recommendations.label: d.
recommendations.text: Instruct the OCAT and City General Services Office (CGSO) to indicate in their PPE records the condition of the PPE using common condition codes as well as the information listed in para. 2.3.2.

observations.title: The Joint Venture Agreement (JVA) entered into by the City of Manila with B. Braun Avitum Philippines, Inc. (BBAPI) does not have certain provisions prescribed in City Ordinance No. 8346 and has unclear and inadequate stipulations which are disadvantageous to the interest of the CGM.
observations.description:
3.1 We reviewed the terms and conditions of the 15-year JVA entered into by the CGM with BBAPI on 13 October 2014 for the establishment, management and operation of a New and Modern Dialysis Center at the Gat Andres Bonifacio Memorial Medical Center (GABMMC) to determine if it conforms to the City Ordinance No. 8346 (JVO) and other pertinent laws, rules and regulation and has no onerous term or condition disadvantageous to the CGM.

3.2 Our review of the JVA showed that it does not have certain provisions prescribed in the JVO and has unclear and inadequate stipulations which are disadvantageous to the interest of the CGM as discussed in the succeeding paragraphs.

JVA Terms and conditions that work against the interest of the CGM

3.3 Section 4.4 of the JVA provides that: “The City of Manila and GABMMC shall provide and perform all laboratory request/requirements of the dialysis patients. Xxx… For laboratory requirements of patients under BBAPI’s program (PhilHealth & PCSO), GABMMC shall provide and extend twenty percent (20%) discount to BBAPI or come up with a special discounted laboratory package for said requirements, whichever is higher.” (emphasis supplied)

3.4 It must be emphasized that the operation of the City hospital, GABMMC, is service rather than profit-oriented such that costing its services should be for cost recovery and not factor in profit. The mandatory granting of this 20-percent discount is a cost burden to GABMMC and, in effect, could be considered as additional investment by the CGM in the joint venture (JV).

3.5 The JVA does not have a provision passing this discount to the patients, thus, only BBAPI is directly benefiting from this privilege (lesser cost for the BBAPI), while the City is left with the burden of shouldering 100 percent of this discount. This effectively reduces the percent-share of the City in the revenue of the JV.

Section 6(1). Specifies the revenue sharing scheme of the JV partners wherein B. Braun Avitum Philippines, Inc. shall be entitled to 75% of standard treatment rate, net of Professional Fee (PF), while the City of Manila thru GABMMC shall be entitled to 25% of standard treatment rate, net of PF or One Hundred Fifty Thousand Pesos (P150,000.00) per month whichever is higher.

Section 6.3. Provides that all revenues outside of the treatment revenue such as sales of pharmaceuticals products, other supplies and consumables, emergency fees and surcharges levied on the patients undergoing treatments in the Dialysis Unit as well as other items/supplies included in the PHIC and PCSO package, such as but not limited to dialyzers, EPO, renal vitamins shall not be covered by the revenue sharing. As such, all revenue coming from the said items shall accrue exclusively to BBAPI. (underscoring supplied)

Section 10. Miscellaneous Provisions. The City of Manila and/or GABMMC shall not set-up and establish a separate Dialysis Unit or allow any other party to set up another Dialysis Unit in the premises of the hospital. (underscoring supplied)

3.6 The CGM’s books of accounts show that its investment in this JV as of 31 December 2020 amounts to P75,613,174.31 and is already 39 percent of the total JV investment at the outset (Table 9). This is on top of: (a) the value of existing structure and land where the dialysis center is situated; (b) the cost of air conditioning system, security and janitorial services for the common areas in the Dialysis Unit; (c) the salary of the dialysis unit medical director; and (d) the foregone revenue in the form of the 20-percent discount for the laboratory requirements of the BBAPI earlier discussed.

Table 9 – Amount and ratio of investment by the JV partners (as of December 31, 2019)

| Parties to the JVA | Investment | Ratio |
| --- | --- | --- |
| B. Braun Avitum Phils., Inc. (equipment and systems) | P120,000,000.00 | 61% |
| City of Manila (building improvements) | 75,613,174.31 | 39% |
| Total | P195,613,174.31 | 100% |

3.7 Given the CGM’s investment in the JV, the revenue share of the CGM is inequitable especially that, (a) based on the JV’s business model, the CGM has provided the BBAPI guaranteed earnings (more so given the monopoly provision in Section 10 of the JVA); and (b) the CGM only shares in the revenue Net of “sales of pharmaceuticals products, other supplies and consumables, emergency fees and surcharges levied on the patients undergoing treatments in the Dialysis Unit as well as other items/supplies included in the PHIC and PCSO package, such as but not limited to dialyzers, EPO, renal vitamins.”

3.8 It must also be pointed out that, while BBAPI had been granted the 20-percent discount on the laboratory requirements referred to GABMMC, the same is NOT even being extended to the City for the cost of pharmaceuticals, supplies and consumables charged to the indigent patients subsidized by the City under its Orange Card Program.

3.9 The JVA passed on to the BBAPI complete control of the procurement and pricing of the pharmaceuticals products, other supplies and consumables arising from the JV’s dialysis operations, which is neither transparent nor competitive. The JVA has not also provided how the City will ensure equitable pricing, safety and quality of these items. This bypasses/circumvents the requirement of RA No. 9184 (Government Procurement Reform Act) enacted to ensure transparency, competitiveness and that the government obtains the most advantageous prices (as provided under Section 2 of its Implementing Rules and Regulations).

3.10 The foregoing terms and conditions work against the interest of the CGM and are valid grounds in the termination of the JVA.

Stipulations prescribed in the JVO but not in the JVA

3.11 Section 9 of the City’s JVO provides that, as far as practicable, the JVA includes certain provisions which are vital in enforcing and managing JV obligations and accountability. However, we noted that some of these provisions are not among those stated in the JVA:

a. Anti-corruption warranties which work against establishing accountability for graft and corruption;

b. The manner of valuation of the JV assets/properties and their ownership during and after the term of the Agreements, thus the: (i) the risk of undervaluation or overvaluation of the interest of the City, and (ii) adverse claims against the City during the dissolution of the JVs; and

c. Procedure for divestment and disposition which will ensure the smooth and efficient auction and abandoning/discarding of JV assets.

Absence of relevant/vital provisions in the JVA

3.12 We have further noted that the JVA failed to include certain provisions vital in protecting the interest of the CGM, its constituents and general public.

a. There is no provision on the imposition of penalty in case of late remittance of City share in the JVA. The absence of such provision would provide BBAPI the luxury of time in the performance of its obligations without being sanctioned for its inability to timely remit the city share, to the detriment of the CGM.

b. Although the applicable treatment rates are specifically provided in the JVA, there is no standard cost therein of the pharmaceutical products, other supplies and consumables that will be levied (per dialysis session) to the patients. Further, there is no provision in the JVA on how the costs of these items are to be regulated by the City. This poses the risk of exorbitant pricing, thus, both detrimental to the dialysis patients and the CGM.

c. There is NO provision on the ownership of the JV data/information generated during the dissolution of the JVA. The lack of this provision is very disadvantageous as this asset is very valuable. The JVA is providing opportunity for B. Braun to arrogate to itself this asset.

d. There is NO clear stipulation as to what will happen to the assets/properties contributed by the City upon dissolution of the JV. This poses serious risk of loss of assets and conflict/disagreement among the JV partners during the dissolution of the JV.

recommendations.label: a.
recommendations.text: increasing the CGM share in the revenue of the JV commensurate to the CGM’s contribution/investment therein; and
recommendations.lead_in: Pursuant to para. 10 of the JVA, we recommended that Management come up with JVA addendum/amendments or similar binding document to correct the provisions and deficiencies therein that work against the interest of the CGM (paragraphs 3.3, 3.10 and 3.11) with the end view of, among others:

recommendations.label: b.
recommendations.text: taking-over the procurement of pharmaceuticals and other consumable items utilized in the dialysis of patients to: (i) conform with the relevant provisions of RA No. 9184; and (ii) ensure reasonable pricing and compliance to quality standards of these items.
recommendations.lead_in: Pursuant to para. 10 of the JVA, we recommended that Management come up with JVA addendum/amendments or similar binding document to correct the provisions and deficiencies therein that work against the interest of the CGM (paragraphs 3.3, 3.10 and 3.11) with the end view of, among others:

recommendations.text: If BBAPI refuses the correction of the foregoing provisions and deficiencies therein that work against the interest of the CGM, terminate the JVA but ensuring in the process the uninterrupted dialysis treatment services by the City.

observations.management_comment: 3.15 The CGM Management submitted its reply on January 2021 together with the B. Braun’s position paper. B. Braun’s position was that, it agreed that the mandatory 20 percent discount granted to B. Braun’s patient in the JVA be removed. It disagreed, however, to our audit recommendation on increasing CGM’s share in the revenue sharing commensurate to its investment. It also disagreed that the CGM take over the procurement pharmaceuticals and other consumable items utilized in the dialysis of patients. It is amenable to the recommendation that the CGM procure the items that are not directly used for the dialysis treatment itself, but may nevertheless be required for the patients as prescribed by the doctors.
observations.auditors_rejoinder:
3.16 Section 8 (f) of the JVO explicitly provides that each party shall be entitled to profits, income and revenues, in proportion to its share. We also anchored our stand to Sections 9 (9) & 10 of the JVO. We have established that B. Braun failed to deliver P47,910,000.00 worth of investments as committed contribution in the JVA making the investment ratio to 52%:48% (B. Braun:CGM).

3.17 B. Braun claims, however, that it placed an additional capital investment in the form of physical improvements, equipment and furniture. Assuming that this is true and correct, the investment ratio should have been: 64%:36%. The ratio derivation is in our reply to the B Braun position paper which had been submitted to the City Legal Office on 28 July 2021.

3.18 We also stand by our previous recommendation that the CGM take over procurement of the items which are not directly used or not standard items used or required for the dialysis treatment.

3.19 We acknowledge that the procurement for the purpose of running the JV project is beyond the ambit of the GPRA. However, for check and balance and for the protection of City’s interest in the JVA, we recommend that the City of Manila place a control mechanism to ensure equitable pricing, safety and quality of the pharmaceutical products, other supplies and consumables arising from the dialysis treatment. We further recommend that the proper operation of said control mechanism be included in the accountability of the City’s representative in the Joint Management Committee.
observations.citation: CY 2020 AAR, Part II, Observation No. 3, pp. 74-79

observations.title: Unsubmitted documents supporting the JVA with JBROS Construction Corporation for the Arroceros Compound Mixed-Use Development prevented the full evaluation of and casts doubt on the validity of the Swiss Challenge to which such joint venture project was subjected. Further, the continuing failure of the JBROS to perform its obligations under the JVA deprives the CGM beneficial use of the Arroceros Compound; and the CGM has not fully protected its interest by its failure to require JBROS to post performance bond covering the period within which the latter is obligated to complete the joint venture project.

recommendations.label: a.
recommendations.text: Submit the documents enumerated in para. 4.7 to establish the validity of the Swiss Challenge;

recommendations.label: b.
recommendations.text: Rescind the JVA in view of the continuing failure of the JBROS to perform its obligations under this JVA and in order to realize beneficial gain from the herein Arroceros Compound; and

recommendations.label: c.
recommendations.text: Prospectively, protect reasonably the interest of the CGM by ensuring that JVAs are adequately bonded.

observations.title: In view of the restrictions posed by the COVID-19 pandemic, the City failed to implement 74 Gender and Development (GAD) program/projects/activities (PPAs) with total corresponding budget of P566.235 million and establish fully the requisite GAD database.
observations.description:
5.1 We audited the GAD funds, programs and activities of the City of Manila pursuant to RA No. 9710 and its IRR, to determine whether the existing laws, rules and regulations on the gender and development are being complied with by the Agency; whether the GAD PPAs implemented have fully addressed the gender issue in accordance with the goal of the program; and the GAD funds were expended for the purpose which they have been appropriated. Our procedures included, among others, analysis of the GBP and validation and evaluation of its delivery.

5.2 The City of Manila has adopted gender mainstreaming as a strategy to promote women’s human rights and eliminate gender discrimination and has been in the process of being a sustainable gender-responsive city.

5.3 On 10 November 2020 the City of Manila passed its GAD Code through Ordinance No. 8681 “An Ordinance Providing for a City Gender and Development Code for the City of Manila and for other purposes”.

5.4 The Manila GAD Plan and Budget (GPB) and GAD Accomplishment Report (GAR) are prepared by each department and submitted to the City Planning Office (CPDO) for consolidation. On 29 January 2020 the CPDO submitted to this Office the GPB together with the Certificate issued by the DILG certifying that the 2020 GPB of the City of Manila was found to be compliant in form and content as provided in the PCW-DILG-DBM-NEDA Joint Memorandum Circular (JMC) No. 2016-01 and PCW-DILG-DBM-NEDA JMC No. 2013-01. The GAR was submitted on 20 May 2021.

5.5 The City allocated P957,688,442.46 for the 120 GAD PPAs programmed for FY 2020. This fund allocation accounted for 5.36 percent of its appropriation of P17,857,086,146.00 for FY 2020 and complies with the prescribed minimum budget.

Non-implementation of 74 GAD PPAs

5.6 Section 6.1 of PCW-DILG-DBM-NEDA JMC No. 2016-01 amending Section 4.1.C.7.1 of PCW-DILG-DBM-NEDA JMC No. 2013-01 states that the Local Chief Executive (LCE) shall issue an appropriate policy directive, copy furnished the DILG Office that conducted the review of the LGU GPB, to disseminate and implement the GPB.

5.7 Section 4.1.C.7.4 of PCW-DILG-DBM-NEDA JMC No. 2013-01 provides that the GFPS shall regularly monitor if the GAD budget is being spent for what it was intended for and check on the actual cost of implementing the GAD activities.

5.8 Analysis of the delivery of the FY 2020 GPB showed that, of the 120 planned PPAs, only 46 PPAs with the budgeted amount of P391,453,658.18 were delivered, thus, leaving 74 with a budget of P566,234,784.28, unimplemented (Table 10).

Table 10 – Schedule GAD PPAs Implemented and Not Implemented

| Particulars | Targeted PPAs | Implemented | Percent | Unimplemented | Percent |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Client Focused | 80 | 32 | 40.00% | 48 | 60.00% |
| Organizational Focused | 38 | 13 | 34.21% | 25 | 65.79% |
| Attributed programs | 2 | 1 | 50.00% | 1 | 50.00% |
| Total | 120 | 46 | 38.33% | 74 | 61.67% |

5.9 We noted 10 GAD-related PPAs which were implemented at a total cost of P54,114,213.73 although these are not among those the GPB for FY 2020. We view this as a positive development considering that more than half of the programmed PPAs were not implemented. Including these 10 PPAs, the City disbursed as at yearend P207,367,964.60 (Table 11).

Table 11 – Schedule of Implemented PPAs Actual Amount Utilized

| Particulars | No. of PPAs | Budgeted Amount | Disbursement |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| PPAS IN GPB |  |  |  |
| Client Focused | 32 | P179,493,270.18 | P138,073,837.09 |
| Organizational Focused | 13 | 10,063,301.00 | 15,121,413.78 |
| Attributed Programs | 1 | 201,897,087.00 | 58,500.00 |
| Sub-Total | 46 | 391,453,658.18 | 153,253,750.87 |
| PPAS NOT IN GPB | 10 | - | 54,114,213.73 |
| Total | 56 | P391,453,658.18 | P207,367,964.60 |

5.10 Because of the community quarantine imposed to contain the COVID-19 pandemic, the implementation of majority of the GAD PPAs were either delayed or halted. During this period work was limited to those essential in addressing the pandemic. Of the GAD budget, P20,115,000.00 was even realigned to respond to this pandemic.

Non-establishment of GAD database

5.11 Chapter VI, Section 36(c) of RA No. 9710 and Rule VI, Section 37 C of the IRR of the same RA provides that all departments, including their attached agencies, offices, bureaus, state universities and colleges, government-owned and controlled corporations, local government units, and other government instrumentalities shall develop and maintain a GAD database containing gender statistics and sex-disaggregated date that have been systematically gathered, regularly updated, and subjected to gender analysis for planning, programming, and policy formulation.

5.12 Section 4.1.B of PCW-DILG-DBM-NEDA JMC No. 2013-01 provides that LGUs, through their Local Planning and Development Offices, shall spearhead the setting up and maintenance of the GAD database to serve as basis for gender-responsive planning, programming and policy formulation. The GAD database, which can either be manually operated or developed through software, shall form part of the overall management information system of the LGU.

5.13 The City’s non-establishment of GAD database had been raised in previous years’ Annual Audit Reports. Verification shows that the CPDO had already sent letter-requests to all department offices and all barangays of the City of Manila to furnish CPDO the relevant data that will be used in the creation of the City’s GAD database. To date, however, such requisite database has not been established yet.

recommendations.text: We recommended that Management implement a catch-up plan for the undelivered GAD PPAs programmed for CY 2020 and establish the requisite GAD database.

observations.management_comment: 5.15 During the exit meeting, Management informed that the City will implement the PPAs as planned, implement virtual GAD programs as a form of compliance.
observations.citation: CY 2020 AAR, Part II, Observation No. 5, pp. 84-86

other_items.section_heading: COMPLIANCE WITH TAX LAWS AND OTHER REGULATORY REQUIREMENTS / Due to BIR, GSIS, Pag-IBIG and PhilHealth

6. The status of remittances of amounts withheld for the accounts of the BIR, GSIS, PhilHealth and Pag-IBIG is in Table 12.

| Unremitted Amount | P23,470,339.19 | P3,835,529.08 | P3,008,523.45 | P15,577,909.65 |

6.1 The unremitted amount to GSIS represents the exception reports from the GSIS - Electronic Billing and Collection System (EBCS). The system validates the Electronic Remittance File (ERF) member records against the GSIS database thru its GSIS matching rules such as the ones in Table 13. It does NOT process the remittances appertaining to the exceptions determined by these rules until resolved. The CGM is regularly working with GSIS to resolve these exceptions.

Table 13 - Matching Rules of the GSIS - EBCS

| Exception Report | Case |
| --- | --- |
| 1. Unmatched Names | Unmatched Name |
|  | Inactive Member |
|  | Inactive MSP |
| 2. Clarificatory Report | New Member |
|  | BP Member Match found in Other Agency |
|  | Invalid BP Number found in ERF |
|  | No Insurance Object found |
| 3. Comparative Report | Underpayment (-) |
|  | Overpayment (+) |

6.2 Taking into account the unresolved exceptions/unremitted balance, the City and GSIS entered into a Memorandum of Agreement on 28 October 2020 for the former to pay within a period of 12 months starting on January 2021 the restructured obligation after the latter condoned 60 percent of the interest incurred from January 2012 to July 2019.
